newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's petrochemicals sale on track - minister.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's petrochemicals sale on track - minister.

text.p: Investors remain interested in Mexico's partial petrochemical sell-off but are waiting for government details on the process, Energy Minister Jesus Reyes Heroles said.
In an interview with foreign correspondents late on Wednesday, Reyes said the 49-percent privatization of Mexico's 10 petrochemical complexes is "advancing at a good rhythm."

After last year's politcally charged battles over an original proposal to completely privatize the secondary petrochemical industry, the government reached a compromise in which Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) will maintain a majority stake in current plants with private firms building and owning any new plants.
Rules for how the plants will be sold and managed are expected to be ready in August with tenders scheduled to be put forward by the government soon afterward.
Currently the Energy Ministry is setting up the petrochemical complexes, preparing labor agreements, contracts and environmental norms for the privatization.

"Almost all big players have shown interest subject to how the final rules come out. All national companies and foreign companies in Mexico plus some foreigners not in Mexico have said they are interested," Reyes said.
One of the major concerns expressed to the ministry is how a private firm would participate in management decisions with state oil and gas monopoly Pemex.
Decisions in the new companies must be made by a 76 percent majority of the board of directors, designed so that the Pemex majority and half of the private participation must agree, Reyes said.
"The Mexican government is not interested in passive investors," he added.
Interested investors will be provided with monthly audited financial statements of the complexes during the first six months of 1997, the minister said.
Labor agreements with the approximately 17,000 petrochemical workers are set through Dec. 31, 1998, after which each company can independently adjust its work contracts.
Reyes said the ministry is still working to set feedstock prices for the new companies and any new plants.

The government already has begun converting six of 10 petrochemical plants into private companies. These complexes -- Cangrejera, Morelos, Cosoleacaque, Escolin, Tula and Camargo -- represent 89 percent of Mexico's total petrochemical sales, Reyes said.

Pajaritos is the last of major complexes to be separated from Pemex along with three of the smaller petrochemical plants, he added. Ministry policy director Raul Livas has estimated the remaining plants will be detached from Pemex by April 1.
